body_markdown:
We often think of posture as something that affects appearance. Sitting up straight can make you look more confident, while slouching can make you appear tired or uncomfortable. But posture is about much more than looking polished.


The way you sit, stand, walk and use everyday devices can influence how your muscles and joints feel. Spending long periods at a desk, looking down at a smartphone or carrying a heavy bag on one shoulder can gradually create habits that place extra strain on the body.


Terms such as “tech neck” and “shrimp posture” have become popular ways of describing some of these modern habits. Although they are not formal medical diagnoses, they describe recognizable positions associated with prolonged device use and sedentary routines.


The good news is that small changes can make a meaningful difference.


## What is “shrimp posture”?


“Shrimp posture” is an informal description for a rounded, hunched position that can develop when someone spends much of the day sitting at a desk or looking at a screen.


The shoulders may move forward, the upper back becomes rounded and the head may drift toward the screen. Some people may also experience tightness around the neck and shoulders or discomfort around the lower back.


Several factors can contribute to this position. A computer monitor that is too low, a chair that does not provide enough support and weak muscles around the upper back and core can all make it easier to fall into a slouched position.


According to Brown University Health, maintaining poor posture for long periods can make it more difficult to change the habit. That does not mean your posture is permanently fixed, however. Adjusting your workspace and developing strength and flexibility can help.


## Why your phone may be contributing to “tech neck”


Smartphones have made it easier than ever to spend hours looking downward.


Whether you are scrolling through social media, replying to messages or watching videos, repeatedly holding your head forward can increase the demands placed on the muscles of the neck.


This is commonly referred to as “tech neck.”


The problem is not necessarily the phone itself. The bigger issue is spending extended periods in the same position without moving or changing your posture.


One simple exercise often recommended for forward-head posture is the chin tuck. Instead of pushing your head forward, gently draw your chin backward, as though you are trying to create a small double chin. The movement should be controlled rather than forced.


Physical therapist Kristen Gasnick, writing for GoodRx, notes that chin tucks can work the deep cervical flexor muscles involved in supporting healthier head and neck positioning.


The goal is not to hold your head perfectly still all day. In fact, regularly changing position is important. Think of posture as something dynamic rather than a single position you must maintain constantly.


## Your desk setup matters


A poorly arranged workstation can encourage slouching without you even realizing it.


If your screen is too low, you may repeatedly tilt your head downward. If your chair is too low or too high, your shoulders, wrists and back may have to compensate.


Try keeping your monitor at a comfortable height so that you can look ahead without constantly bending your neck. Your feet should have stable support, while your shoulders should remain relaxed rather than raised toward your ears.


It is also useful to stand up regularly. Even a few minutes of movement between periods of sitting can break up long stretches of inactivity.


Rather than searching for one “perfect” sitting position, focus on variety. Alternate between sitting, standing and walking whenever possible.


## Strength can help support better posture


Posture is not simply about reminding yourself to “sit straight.”


Muscle strength plays an important role in helping the body maintain comfortable positions.


The muscles around your core, back and shoulders contribute to stability. If these areas are weak or become fatigued quickly, maintaining an upright position may become more difficult.


Orthopedic surgeon Dr Sabrina Strickland has highlighted the connection between core strength and posture, with exercises such as planks, sit-ups and Russian twists among activities that can strengthen the midsection.


You do not necessarily need an elaborate workout routine. Consistent strength training that includes the core and upper body can be a useful part of a broader approach to physical health.


## Do not forget your shoulders and chest


Long periods of sitting can also leave the chest and shoulders feeling tight.


Harvard Medical School recommends a simple stretch involving bringing the arms behind the body and holding the elbows or forearms. The position can help stretch the chest area, particularly if sitting at a desk has left you feeling hunched forward.


Another option is gently clasping your hands behind your back and lifting them slightly while keeping the movement comfortable.


Stretching should never be painful. If a movement causes sharp pain, numbness or unusual symptoms, stop and consider speaking with a qualified healthcare professional.


## Could your handbag be affecting your posture?


Your posture is not only influenced by what happens at your desk.


Carrying a heavy handbag or shoulder bag on the same side every day can place uneven demands on your body. You may unconsciously raise one shoulder, lean to one side or change the way you walk to compensate for the weight.


A simple solution is to reduce the weight you carry whenever possible.


Switching shoulders can also prevent one side of the body from constantly carrying the load. For people who regularly transport heavier items, a well-fitted backpack that distributes weight across both shoulders may be a more balanced option.


## Small changes can add up


Improving posture does not require sitting rigidly upright from morning until night.


Instead, focus on everyday habits.


Raise your screen if you regularly look downward. Take movement breaks during long periods of sitting. Keep your phone closer to eye level when practical. Strengthen your core and upper back. Stretch areas that feel tight. Avoid carrying unnecessarily heavy bags on one side.


Perhaps most importantly, pay attention to discomfort before it becomes a persistent problem.


Posture is influenced by many factors, including muscle strength, flexibility, work environment, activity levels and individual anatomy. There is no single position that is ideal for everyone.


The best posture may simply be your next posture. Regular movement and changing positions throughout the day can be more realistic and beneficial than trying to hold yourself perfectly still.


## Final thoughts


Modern life has made prolonged sitting and screen use almost unavoidable for many people. That does not mean neck, shoulder or back discomfort has to become a permanent part of daily life.


Your smartphone, laptop and even your handbag can influence the way you position your body, but they do not have to dictate it.


Start with manageable changes. Adjust your workspace, move more often, strengthen the muscles that support your body and be conscious of how you carry everyday items.


Good posture is less about forcing yourself into a rigid pose and more about creating an environment where your body can move comfortably and regularly.


### Sources


1. Cleveland Clinic, “Health Effects of Poor Posture.”
2. Brown University Health, “Posture and How It Affects Your Health.”
3. Harvard Medical School, “Is It Too Late to Save Your Posture?”
4. The Independent, published 25 August 2026.

Exercises and stretches should be performed within a comfortable range and stopped if they cause pain.
